tagline: Mountain roads connect railway villages and communities reshaped by city water.
intro: The Catskill Mountains Scenic Byway winds through mountains, waterways and rolling farmland between Andes and Olive. It mainly follows Route 28, with short extensions on Routes 42 and 214. New York’s Department of Transportation identifies its scenic and historic qualities, celebrating the Catskill Park, the New York City watershed and the region’s historic railroads.

Travel here once meant rough roads, followed by a plank road from Kingston to Pine Hill whose maintenance was paid for at tollgates. Rail service helped Pine Hill become a tourist community. In 2008, municipalities along the Route 28 corridor appointed representatives to a collaborative formed to protect and promote its assets and advance economic projects. The byway’s organizing coalition brought together the towns of Olive, Shandaken, Middletown and Andes and the villages of Fleischmanns and Margaretville.

From Andes, Route 28 leads southeast to Margaretville in the East Branch Delaware River valley. Continue past Fleischmanns and Pine Hill to Phoenicia, where Stony Clove Creek joins the Esopus. Phoenicia’s center lies just off Route 28 at the Route 214 junction, beneath Mount Tremper, Romer Mountain and Sheridan Mountain. The eastern stretch reaches Boiceville and Shokan, communities relocated for the Ashokan Reservoir.

moments.title: Fleischmanns
moments.text: Fleischmanns Park was once a place where baseball players prepared for the regular season. Honus Wagner was among them. In May 1914, Julius Fleischmann gave the park to the village, attaching conditions that it remain a park and athletic grounds, be maintained and never be sold or sublet. The park had been known as the Mountain Athletic Club and occupied the north side of Wagner Avenue. His gift originally required free public access, too. In 1934, the village obtained permission from the heirs to remove that requirement so it could charge admission for certain events.

moments.title: Phoenicia
moments.text: The wooden Phoenicia depot dates to 1899, replacing the hamlet’s first station, a masonry building from 1870. The later station served both the main line and a branch carrying passengers toward mountain resorts. Its relocation and five tracks relieved backups from trains that had stretched onto the nearby Esopus Creek bridge. Only one of the station’s former five tracks remains beside it. Its bluestone foundation gives way to wood-shingled walls, with decorative brackets beneath the eaves. The depot now houses the Empire State Railway Museum. Its deep roof overhang shelters a wooden platform, and the former ticket office retains brass window bars.
moments.notice: The depot’s deep roof overhang shelters its wooden platform.

moments.title: Shokan
moments.text: Shokan moved because New York City’s water supply took its former site. Between 1907 and 1915, the city’s Board of Water Supply built the Ashokan Reservoir by impounding Esopus Creek. The water covered 12 communities and thousands of acres of farmland; approximately 2,000 residents were displaced. Residents fought the city’s eminent domain proceedings, and the last land claims were not settled until 1940. Roads were removed or abandoned, and cemeteries were relocated. Shokan is among the relocated communities along the reservoir’s banks; historical markers on Routes 28 and 28A identify others that disappeared.
